description: Sprint 104 regression fixture: shared authoritative corpus (three synthetic diagnostic-test datasets) and the verbatim specification_text of live Stage 4 commissions comm_5, comm_7, comm_8 and comm_9 (0-based commission indices 4, 6, 7, 8), which were falsely rejected, plus comm_4 and comm_6 as controls. The commissions were falsely rejected as specification_text_duplicates_full_shared_source. The trailing COMPONENT_LEARNING_OUTCOMES marker blocks are omitted (they contain no corpus text).
shared_content:
ILLUSTRATIVE SHARED CORPUS: FICTIONAL HEALTHCARE SCENARIO AND SYNTHETIC DIAGNOSTIC TEST DATA

All healthcare scenarios, people, conditions and numerical data in this corpus are fictional and constructed solely for introductory learning. They do not describe an actual diagnostic test, clinical investigation or published research study. The figures must not be used to inform clinical decisions.

RECURRING SCENARIO
A fictional healthcare service is evaluating a diagnostic test for an unnamed health condition. The test reports either a positive or a negative result. For the purposes of these illustrative datasets, actual condition status is established independently using an assumed reliable reference procedure. Learners are not required to understand the clinical details of either procedure. The educational focus is the relationship between reported test results, actual condition status and population prevalence.

REPRESENTATIONAL CONVENTION
Use consistently labelled two-by-two tables with actual condition status in columns and reported test result in rows. Include row totals, column totals and the overall population total. Use the same terminology throughout: true positive (TP), false positive (FP), true negative (TN), false negative (FN). Do not rely on colour alone to distinguish categories. Natural frequencies are the primary representation; percentages may supplement them. Where percentages are rounded, identify them as approximate.

DATASET A: BASELINE POPULATION
Population size: 200 people.
People with the condition: 100.
People without the condition: 100.
Positive results among people with the condition (TP): 90.
Positive results among people without the condition (FP): 20.
Negative results among people with the condition (FN): 10.
Negative results among people without the condition (TN): 80.
Total positive results: 110.
Total negative results: 90.
Prevalence: 100/200 = 50%.
Sensitivity: 90/100 = 90%.
Specificity: 80/100 = 80%.
False negative rate: 10/100 = 10%.
False positive rate: 20/100 = 20%.
Positive predictive value: 90/110, approximately 81.8%.
Negative predictive value: 80/90, approximately 88.9%.
Proportion of positive results that are false: 20/110, approximately 18.2%.
Proportion of negative results that are false: 10/90, approximately 11.1%.

FICTIONAL INDIVIDUAL EXAMPLES FROM DATASET A
Person A: has the condition and receives a positive result; true positive.
Person B: does not have the condition and receives a positive result; false positive.
Person C: has the condition and receives a negative result; false negative.
Person D: does not have the condition and receives a negative result; true negative.
These examples illustrate the four possible classifications. They are members of the illustrative population, not additional observations to be added to its totals.

DATASET B: LOWER-PREVALENCE POPULATION
The same fictional diagnostic test is applied to a second population of equal size in which the condition is less common. For this comparison, sensitivity and specificity are assumed to remain unchanged. This is a simplifying assumption for the learning example, not a universal property of diagnostic tests.
Population size: 200 people.
People with the condition: 20.
People without the condition: 180.
Positive results among people with the condition (TP): 18.
Positive results among people without the condition (FP): 36.
Negative results among people with the condition (FN): 2.
Negative results among people without the condition (TN): 144.
Total positive results: 54.
Total negative results: 146.
Prevalence: 20/200 = 10%.
Sensitivity: 18/20 = 90%.
Specificity: 144/180 = 80%.
False negative rate: 2/20 = 10%.
False positive rate: 36/180 = 20%.
Positive predictive value: 18/54, approximately 33.3%.
Negative predictive value: 144/146, approximately 98.6%.
Proportion of positive results that are false: 36/54, approximately 66.7%.
Proportion of negative results that are false: 2/146, approximately 1.4%.

AUTHORITATIVE COMPARISON OF DATASETS A AND B
Both populations contain 200 people. Prevalence decreases from 50% to 10%. Sensitivity remains 90% and specificity remains 80%. Positive predictive value decreases from approximately 81.8% to 33.3%. Negative predictive value increases from approximately 88.9% to 98.6%. In Population B, 36 of the 54 positive results are false positives, compared with 20 of the 110 positive results in Population A. The false positive rate remains 20% in both populations because its denominator is all people without the condition. The proportion of positive results that are false changes because its denominator is all people receiving a positive result. Lower prevalence means fewer people with the condition are available to generate true positives and more people without the condition are available to generate false positives. The same underlying error rates therefore produce a different composition of reported results.

DATASET C: INDEPENDENT TRANSFER SITUATION
A third fictional healthcare service uses the same illustrative test in a population with a different prevalence. A person from this population receives a negative test result and asks whether this establishes that they do not have the condition. Their actual condition status is unknown to the learner. Assume the person belongs to the population described and no additional individual clinical information is available. This situation is reserved for the final independent interpretation commission and must not be disclosed in earlier components.
Population size: 200 people.
People with the condition: 40.
People without the condition: 160.
Positive results among people with the condition (TP): 36.
Positive results among people without the condition (FP): 32.
Negative results among people with the condition (FN): 4.
Negative results among people without the condition (TN): 128.
Total positive results: 68.
Total negative results: 132.
Prevalence: 40/200 = 20%.
Sensitivity: 36/40 = 90%.
Specificity: 128/160 = 80%.
False negative rate: 4/40 = 10%.
False positive rate: 32/160 = 20%.
Positive predictive value: 36/68, approximately 52.9%.
Negative predictive value: 128/132, approximately 97.0%.
Proportion of positive results that are false: 32/68, approximately 47.1%.
Proportion of negative results that are false: 4/132, approximately 3.0%.

AUTHORITATIVE INTERPRETATION OF DATASET C
Among the 132 people receiving negative results, 128 do not have the condition and 4 do. A negative result therefore provides evidence that the condition is absent in this illustrative population, but it does not establish absence with certainty. The relevant predictive proportion is 128/132, approximately 97.0%, rather than specificity (80%) or sensitivity (90%). The remaining 4/132 negative results are false negatives. These population-level figures support an appropriately qualified interpretation for someone drawn from the described population; they do not establish the actual condition status of a particular individual. No clinical management recommendation is required.

CONSISTENCY AND DISCLOSURE RULES
Dataset A is introduced in the first commission and reused through the introductory classification, accuracy and predictive-value commissions. Dataset B is introduced only when prevalence becomes the explicit focus. Dataset C is reserved for independent transfer. Do not introduce additional numerical datasets, change population sizes, alter frequencies or substitute real clinical conditions. The complete corpus is available to downstream authors for consistency, but each learner-facing component should expose only the material necessary for its educational job. Do not reveal later interpretations or assessment answers prematurely. All numerical tables and accompanying explanations must preserve the exact frequencies and mathematically consistent derived values above.

commissions.comm_4: Create a focused diagnostic accuracy practice experience using the familiar Dataset A. The educational job is to apply the modelled reasoning from the preceding component and demonstrate appropriate numerator and denominator selection. Learners already know the four diagnostic result categories, the meanings of sensitivity and specificity and their relationship to complementary error rates. Present the established two-by-two table with its original frequencies and totals, but do not reproduce the worked calculations or reveal the derived accuracy measures before the learner attempts the task. Retain concise definitions of sensitivity and specificity as appropriate scaffolding. Require learners to construct or select the numerical proportion for sensitivity and calculate its value, then identify the correct interpretation of that value. Require the equivalent performance for specificity. Structure the practice so that denominator selection is visible rather than assessing only the final percentage, since both condition-based groups happen to contain 100 people in Dataset A. The response mechanism should therefore distinguish the reference group itself, not merely its numerical size. Learners should identify the relevant group and subset, obtain the percentage and distinguish its meaning from plausible misconceptions. Use short structured responses rather than extended authored explanations. Feedback must explain the correct reference group and calculation for each measure, distinguish arithmetic mistakes from conceptual mistakes, and address inappropriate use of all tested people or all people with a particular reported result as the denominator. Include concise correction guidance for incorrect interpretations. Do not add new datasets, separate complementary-rate calculations or predictive-value teaching. Internal workload allocation: approximately 3 minutes for revisiting the familiar table, selecting reference groups, constructing the two proportions, performing the simple calculations and making interpretation decisions, followed by 1 minute for feedback engagement and targeted correction. These are integrated calculation-and-interpretation performances, not separate extended tasks. Do not expose the internal timing breakdown in learner-facing prose. No learner-authored text artefact is required.
commissions.comm_5: Create a concise conceptual expository experience that establishes positive and negative predictive values through a change in the question asked of familiar diagnostic evidence. Assume learners can distinguish the four result categories, calculate sensitivity and specificity and interpret these measures using condition-based reference groups. Revisit Dataset A without repeating introductory explanations or treating the table as unfamiliar evidence. Begin from the perspective of someone who knows their reported result but does not know whether they have the condition. Contrast the question addressed by sensitivity with the question addressed by positive predictive value. Use the familiar counts to demonstrate that sensitivity considers the 90 true positives among the 100 people with the condition, whereas positive predictive value considers those same 90 true positives among all 110 people receiving positive results. Explain that the latter proportion is 90/110, approximately 81.8%. Establish the corresponding distinction between specificity and negative predictive value: specificity considers the 80 true negatives among the 100 people without the condition, whereas negative predictive value considers those 80 true negatives among all 90 people receiving negative results. Explain that the latter proportion is 80/90, approximately 88.9%. Make the changed reference groups explicit and connect each predictive proportion to a plain-language interpretation. Use natural frequencies as the primary representation, with rounded percentages as supporting information. Explain that predictive values describe the composition of groups receiving particular results in the supplied population and do not establish the actual condition status of a particular person. Avoid formal conditional probability notation, Bayesian formulae and additional accuracy measures. Do not introduce the prevalence comparison yet. Internal workload allocation: approximately 1 minute for retrieving the meaning of sensitivity and specificity and revisiting the familiar table, followed by 2 minutes for the conceptual contrast and modelled interpretation. Do not add a separate learner calculation or response task because application follows in the next commission. Do not expose the internal timing breakdown in learner-facing prose.
commissions.comm_6: Create a focused practice experience requiring learners to determine and interpret positive and negative predictive proportions from the familiar Dataset A. Assume the distinction between condition-based accuracy measures and result-based predictive measures has already been explained and modelled. Present the familiar table with its original frequencies and totals, but withhold the calculated predictive values until feedback. Require learners to identify the proportion of people receiving positive results who actually have the condition and the proportion of people receiving negative results who do not have the condition. Use concise structured responses that make numerator, denominator and reference-group selection apparent. Accept natural-frequency expressions or fractions as complete numerical answers; do not require learners to calculate awkward decimal percentages manually. Include a compact interpretation decision for each proportion so that learners demonstrate its meaning rather than merely identify table cells. Use plausible incorrect interpretations involving sensitivity, specificity or the wrong denominator. Feedback should explain why the correct proportions are 90/110 and 80/90 respectively, supply the approximate percentages where useful, and distinguish these proportions from sensitivity and specificity. Reinforce that some people with positive results do not have the condition and some people with negative results do. Avoid a separate extended written explanation, additional calculation sequence or new population. Internal workload allocation: approximately 2 minutes for revisiting the familiar evidence and completing the two integrated proportion-and-interpretation performances, followed by 1 minute for explanatory feedback and targeted correction. Do not expose the internal timing breakdown in learner-facing prose. No learner-authored text artefact is required.
commissions.comm_7: Create a concise comparative expository experience introducing prevalence as a population characteristic that influences the interpretation of diagnostic test results. Assume learners understand the four result categories, sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values, including the different reference groups used to determine these measures. Re-present familiar Dataset A alongside previously unseen Dataset B from the locked shared authoritative material. Both populations contain 200 people and use the same fictional diagnostic test. Explain prevalence as the proportion of people in a population who have the condition. Establish that prevalence is 50% in Population A and 10% in Population B. Present consistently organised, accessible tables with all four result frequencies and totals. Supply the calculated prevalence, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and negative predictive value for each population so that learners do not need to reconstruct the datasets or perform repetitive arithmetic. Make clear that sensitivity remains 90% and specificity remains 80% in both populations by design. Explicitly identify this as a simplifying assumption for the comparison rather than a universal property of diagnostic tests. Direct attention to what changes and what remains constant, particularly the different numbers of people with and without the condition and the resulting changes in the composition of positive and negative results. Establish the comparison framework without fully supplying the causal explanation that learners will construct in the next commission. Do not introduce Dataset C. Internal workload allocation: approximately 2 minutes for first-pass inspection of the unfamiliar Dataset B and comparison with the familiar Dataset A, followed by 1 minute for retrieving and connecting established concepts. Keep explanatory prose and the amount of displayed numerical information proportionate to this allocation. Use natural frequencies alongside rounded percentages and accessible labels. No separate calculation task, extended authored response or full feedback cycle is required. Do not expose the internal timing breakdown in learner-facing prose.
commissions.comm_8: Create a comparative reasoning practice experience using Datasets A and B from the locked shared authoritative material. Both datasets are now familiar evidence because the preceding commission introduced their comparison, supplied their calculated measures and established the assumption of constant sensitivity and specificity. Do not repeat the full explanatory grounding or require learners to calculate every measure again. Retain both accessible tables and the relevant supplied predictive proportions. Require learners to identify the direction of change in positive predictive value and negative predictive value as prevalence decreases from 50% to 10%. Then require a concise learner-authored explanation, normally one or two sentences, of why a positive result has a different meaning in the lower-prevalence population despite unchanged sensitivity and specificity. The explanation must use relevant numerical evidence from the comparison and connect the change in population composition to the balance of true and false positive results. Avoid prompts that prescribe the causal explanation or provide a sentence with the substantive reasoning already completed. Declare the learner-authored explanation using elicitation_id E8. This is the sole Journal-producing text elicitation in this commission. Provide explanatory feedback after the learner has constructed their response. Feedback should identify the decrease in positive predictive value from approximately 81.8% to 33.3% and the increase in negative predictive value from approximately 88.9% to 98.6%. Explain that the lower-prevalence population contains fewer people with the condition and more people without it, producing fewer true positives and more false positives under the unchanged accuracy assumptions. Use the comparison between 20 false positives among 110 positive results and 36 false positives among 54 positive results to illustrate the changing composition of positive results. Explicitly distinguish the unchanged false positive rate of 20% from the changing proportion of positive results that are false. Supply a concise worked explanation and guidance for identifying whether the learner's response makes the causal connection. Permit targeted refinement of the existing response without requiring a separate full rewrite. The learner-authored explanation should remain available as current editable work for the journey-level Learning Journal. Internal workload allocation: approximately 3 minutes for revisiting the familiar evidence, identifying both directions of change and constructing the concise comparative explanation, followed by 1 minute for engaging with feedback and making any small correction. Reasoning and explanation construction constitute one integrated performance and should not be charged as separate tasks. Do not add extended reflection, further calculations, a second authored explanation or a Journal-specific writing task. Do not expose the internal timing breakdown in learner-facing prose.
commissions.comm_9: Create a compact formative assessment experience whose principal educational job is to elicit interpretable evidence of integrated diagnostic test interpretation and limited near transfer. This is not a high-stakes assessment, clinical decision-making exercise or claim of independent clinical competence. Assume learners have completed classification practice, calculated and interpreted sensitivity and specificity, determined predictive proportions, and explained how prevalence influences predictive values. Introduce the previously unseen fictional situation and Dataset C from the locked shared authoritative material. A person from the described population has received a negative diagnostic test result and asks whether this establishes that they do not have the condition. Their actual condition status is unknown. Present the familiar two-by-two table structure with Dataset C's exact frequencies and totals. Supply prevalence, sensitivity, specificity and both predictive values, using natural frequencies and appropriately rounded percentages. Do not identify which measure learners should use, highlight the correct reference group or supply the substantive interpretation before the learner responds. Require one concise learner-authored interpretation, normally two or three sentences, that addresses the person's question using relevant numerical evidence and explains what the negative result supports and what uncertainty remains. Declare this response using elicitation_id E9. This is the sole Journal-producing text elicitation in this commission. The performance should require selection and interpretation of appropriate evidence rather than further lengthy calculation. Keep the task independent: do not display the learner's earlier comparative explanation or any previous learner response. Provide a concise worked interpretation after the response has been constructed. The worked interpretation must establish that 128 of the 132 people receiving negative results do not have the condition, approximately 97%, while 4 of the 132 negative results are false negatives. Explain that the negative result supports the conclusion that the condition is absent in this illustrative population but does not establish absence with certainty for the individual. Distinguish the relevant negative predictive proportion from the sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 80%. Provide concise self-evaluation criteria addressing selection of the appropriate reference group, accurate use of numerical evidence, recognition of residual uncertainty and avoidance of unsupported certainty. Integrate the worked interpretation and criteria so they complement rather than duplicate one another. Permit learners to reconsider and make a targeted refinement to their existing response after feedback. Do not require a separate reflective response, second case, full rewrite, clinical recommendation or additional calculation task. Retain the current editable learner response as the declared artefact for the journey-level Learning Journal. Do not claim that the runtime preserves a pre-feedback version or automatically evaluates the learner's authored text. Internal workload allocation: approximately 1 minute for first-pass inspection of the unfamiliar situation and evidence, 2 minutes for the integrated reasoning-and-response performance, and 2 minutes for worked feedback, self-evaluation, targeted refinement and consolidation. Keep the evidence and response demand compact enough to support this allocation. Do not expose the internal timing breakdown in learner-facing prose. Conclude by reinforcing that diagnostic test results provide evidence about condition status rather than automatically establishing it.
